source_text: His patientiae uiribus secatur Esaias et de domino non tacet, lapidatur Stephanus et ueniam hostibus suis postulat. o felicissimum illum quoque, qui omnem patientiae speciem aduersus omnem diaboli uim expunxit! quem non abactae greges, non] illae in pecore diuitiae, non filii uno ruinae impetu adempti, non ipsius denique corporis in uulnere crucia. tus a patientia fide domino dedita exclusit, quem diabolus totis uiribus frustra cecidit. neque enim a respectu dei tot doloribus auocatus ille est, sed constitit nobis in exemplum et testimonium tam spiritu quam carne tam animo quam corpore patientiae perpetrandae, ut neque damnis saecularium nec amissionibus carissimorum nec corporis quidem conflictationibus succidamus. quale in illo uiro feretrum deus de diabolo extruxit, quale uexillum de inimico gloriae suae extulit, cum ille homo ad omnem acerbum nuntium nihil\' ex ore promeret nisi deo gratias, cum uxorem iam malis: delassatam et ad praua remedia suadentem execraretur! quid ridebat deus, quid dissecabatur malus, cum Iob inmundum ulceris sui redundantiam magna aequanimitate destringeret, cum erumpentes bestiolas inde in eosdem specus et pastus refossae carnis ludendo reuocaret! itaque operarius ille uictoriae dei retusis omnibus iaculis temptationum lorica clipeoque patientiae et integritatem mox corporis a deo recuperauit et quae amiserat conduplicata possedit et si filios quoque restitui uoluisset, pater iterum uocaretur. sed maluit in illo die reddi sibi: tantum gaudii, securus de domino, distulit: sustinuit iam uoluntariam orbitatem, ne sine aliqua patientia uiueret.
thought_title: Job as the trophy of patience
orientation: Tertullian is giving examples of bodily patience, moving from Isaiah and Stephen to Job, whom the devil attacked in every way but could not move from patience.
pass_a_gloss: By the powers of patience Isaiah is sawn in two and does not keep silent about the Lord; Stephen is stoned and asks pardon for his enemies. O most blessed also that man, who worked out every kind of patience against every force of the devil! Whom the driven-away herds did not exclude from patience, nor those riches in cattle, nor the sons taken away by one rush of ruin, nor finally the torments of his own body in a wound, from patience pledged to God by faith; whom the devil struck with all his forces in vain. For he was not called away from regard for God by so many pains, but he stood for us as an example and testimony of patience to be accomplished as much in spirit as in flesh, as much in mind as in body, so that we may not fall under losses of worldly things nor under the taking away of dearest ones nor indeed under the batterings of the body. What a bier God built for himself from the devil in that man, what a standard he raised from the enemy of his own glory, when that man at every bitter message brought forth nothing from his mouth except thanks to God, when he cursed his wife, already worn out by evils and urging him to wicked remedies! How God laughed, how the evil one was cut to pieces, when Job scraped off the unclean overflow of his ulcer with great equanimity, when he called back the little creatures bursting out from there into the same caves and pastures of the dug-up flesh by playing with them! And so that workman of God's victory, with all the darts of temptations blunted, by the breastplate and shield of patience both soon recovered the soundness of his body from God and possessed doubled what he had lost, and if he had wished his sons also to be restored, he would be called father again. But he preferred that so much joy be returned to him on that day; secure about the Lord, he put it off; he endured now a voluntary childlessness, so that he might not live without some patience.

choices.why: The image is of a funeral bier, a display of the devil's defeat carried as a trophy; 'bier' keeps the concrete object and the triumph-over-death irony.
A military banner raised in victory; 'standard' preserves the military image of God raising a sign from the defeated enemy.
The verb means to cut apart; the passive shows the devil being torn apart by Job's patience, matching the violent imagery.
The verb means to strip or scrape off; Job is removing the overflow from his ulcer, and the physical action should be kept literal.
Job is the agent through whom God's victory is worked out; 'workman' keeps the labor image and the genitive of the victory belonging to God.
The word means doubled or multiplied; 'doubled' is the plain literal sense of Job's restored possessions.

pass_b_english: Isaiah is sawn in two by the powers of patience, and he does not stop speaking about the Lord. Stephen is stoned, and he asks forgiveness for his enemies. Oh, how blessed was that man too, who worked out every form of patience against every force of the devil! His flocks were driven away, his wealth in livestock was taken, his children were snatched from him in a single crashing blow, and then his own body was tortured with wounds—yet none of this shut him out from the patience he had given to God in faith. The devil struck him with all his strength and accomplished nothing. He was not called away from looking to God by so many sorrows; instead, he stood as an example and witness for us, showing that patience must be carried through in spirit and flesh, in mind and body alike, so that we do not collapse under losses of worldly goods, or the loss of those we love most, or even the afflictions of the body itself. What a bier God built from the devil in that man! What a standard he raised from the enemy of his glory, when that man, at every bitter message, let nothing come from his mouth except thanks to God (Job 1:21), and when he cursed his wife, already worn out by evils and urging him toward wicked remedies (Job 2:9-10)! How God laughed, how the evil one was cut to pieces, when Job scraped off the foul overflow of his ulcer with great composure, and when he calmly called the little creatures bursting out of it back into the same hollows and feeding places of his reopened flesh! And so that workman of God's victory, having blunted every dart of temptation with the breastplate and shield of patience, soon recovered the wholeness of his body from God, and possessed double what he had lost (Job 42:10). And if he had wished his children also to be restored, he could have been called father again. But he preferred to have them returned to him on that day; he postponed such great joy, confident in the Lord. He endured a voluntary childlessness for a time, so that he would not live without some patience.

last_rejected.quote: and possessed double what he had lost (Job 42:10). And if he had wished his children also to be restored, he could have been called father again.
last_rejected.source_quote: et si filios quoque restitui uoluisset, pater iterum uocaretur
last_rejected.why: Source says 'if HE [God] had wished children also to be restored'; English says 'if HE [Job] had wished'
last_rejected.fix: And if God had wished his children also to be restored, he could have been called father again.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin subjunctive voluisset refers to the same subject (the worker/Job), not God; translation matches.

last_rejected.quote: But he preferred to have them returned to him on that day
last_rejected.source_quote: sed maluit in illo die reddi sibi
last_rejected.why: Subject is God, not Job; God preferred to receive them back on that day.
last_rejected.fix: But God preferred to have them returned to him on that day
last_rejected.ruling: maluit with reddi sibi means the worker preferred his children be returned to him; agency correctly rendered.

last_rejected.quote: His flocks were driven away, his wealth in livestock was taken, his children were snatched from him in a single crashing blow, and then his own body was tortured with wounds—yet none of this shut him out
last_rejected.source_quote: quem non abactae greges, non illae in pecore diuitiae, non filii uno ruinae impetu adempti, non ipsius denique corporis in uulnere crucia
last_rejected.why: Latin uses "non" indicating he was NOT deprived; English flips the meaning.
last_rejected.fix: His flocks were not driven away, nor his livestock wealth taken, nor his children snatched in a single blow, nor his own body wounded—yet none of this shut him out
last_rejected.ruling: Each 'non' negates that these trials excluded him from patience; 'none of this shut him out' correctly renders the series of negative clauses.

last_rejected.quote: The devil struck him with all his strength and accomplished nothing.
last_rejected.source_quote: quem diabolus totis uiribus frustra cecidit
last_rejected.why: Latin says the devil fell in vain with all his strength, not that he struck him.
last_rejected.fix: The devil, with all his strength, fell in vain.
last_rejected.ruling: 'cecidit' here means 'struck down/attacked,' not 'fell'; 'frustra' = 'in vain/accomplished nothing.' Translation is correct.

problems.quote: he playfully called the little creatures bursting out of it back into the same hollows
problems.why: Bizarre image of Job playfully addressing worms in his sores.

edits.old: he playfully called the little creatures bursting out of it back into the same hollows
edits.new: he calmly called the little creatures bursting out of it back into the same hollows

fixed: The source reads 'ludendo reuocaret' — 'called back by playing with them.' The adverb 'ludendo' (from 'ludere', to play) does mean playfully, but in context it describes Job's calm, almost detached composure in dealing with the worms, not a bizarre playful address. The English 'playfully' misstates the tone; 'calmly' better conveys the equanimity Tertullian is praising, consistent with 'magna aequanimitate' earlier in the sentence.
